name: Dihydroquercetin glucoside

lead: Dihydroquercetin glucoside (DHQG) is a sugar-linked form of taxifolin, a plant flavonoid, and is one of the two components of the Redensyl hair-growth active. People use Redensyl serums hoping for thicker-looking scalp hair.

The marketing claim is that it stimulates follicle stem cells. No study of DHQG alone was found; small studies have tested finished serums, and a 2025 review discusses Redensyl among topical hair actives.

paras: It is used as a leave-on scalp serum, usually as part of a daily or regular routine and often alongside other thinning-hair products. Users typically judge results over several months.
Taxifolin is reported as non-mutagenic in bacterial tests. No human safety data for DHQG itself were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: DHQG is one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic active in serums for thinning hair. The claim is that it stimulates follicle stem cells for thicker-looking hair. The supporting data come from Redensyl-containing serums rather than the component alone.

lead: Dihydroquercetin glucoside (DHQG) is described in hair-care marketing as one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic active added to scalp serums and lotions with the aim of supporting hair growth and a fuller-looking head of hair; the other component is EGCG-glucoside. DHQG is a glucoside of dihydroquercetin, also called taxifolin, a flavanonol found in Siberian larch, milk thistle and other plants.[1]

No clinical study of DHQG on its own has been published. It has been tested only as part of finished products: a 2020 randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study of a lotion combining Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 in 44 people with androgenetic alopecia reported improvements, and a 2025 study of a rosemary and Redensyl serum in healthy women evaluated hair outcomes for a multi-ingredient product.[2] A 2025 review discusses Redensyl among topical hair actives.

paras: Taxifolin is a flavonoid that, according to Wikipedia, has mainly laboratory and animal findings, including reports of chemopreventive and lipid-lowering activity and inhibition of melanogenesis in one study; the article does not mention hair.[1]

DHQG is sold as part of Redensyl in over-the-counter scalp serums and lotions, usually alongside other actives. A 2020 trial of a Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 lotion used twice daily for 24 weeks randomized 44 patients to active or vehicle; of 26 active-treated patients, 7.7 percent had great improvement, 73.1 percent moderate improvement and 19.2 percent remained stable, with the median anagen-to-telogen ratio rising from 2.25 to 6.02 and no significant adverse events reported.[2] Because the lotion contained more than one active, results cannot be assigned to DHQG itself.

No studies found for DHQG alone. A randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study of a Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 lotion in 44 patients with androgenetic alopecia reported improvement over 24 weeks,[2] and a 2025 study of a rosemary and Redensyl serum in healthy women evaluated hair outcomes for a multi-ingredient product. A 2025 review covers Redensyl among topical hair actives.
